infernet

About the package

infernet is the inferential layer of the stocnet ecosystem. It asks whether what we see in a network could have come about by chance. Each of its answers compares an observed value with a distribution of values from networks that a null hypothesis allows: random networks, networks with the same degrees, or the same network with its nodes relabelled.

The package has five families of functions:

  • Tests of a network statistic, of a model’s parameters, or of a model’s fit: test_random(), test_configuration(), test_permutation(), test_parameter(), test_time(), test_gof(), and test_distributions().
  • Specification of a formula that one model can read and another can fit: specify_mrqap() and specify_ergm().
  • Regression of a network on nodal and dyadic covariates, by multiple regression quadratic assignment procedure (MRQAP): estimate_mrqap() and control_mrqap().
  • Diffusion, simulated many times, to test a model of diffusion against: play_diffusions().
  • Results, as tidy data frames: tidy(), glance(), and predict().

Every function accepts the networks that manynet reads: matrices, edgelists, igraph, network, and tidygraph objects, one-mode or two-mode, directed or undirected, cross-sectional or longitudinal.

Where infernet sits in stocnet

infernet does one job, and leaves the other jobs to its neighbours:

  • {manynet} holds the data: the network classes, the conversions between them, and the networks that the examples below use.
  • {netrics} holds the measures, such as net_by_heterophily(), that the tests take as their statistic.
  • {autograph} draws the results: plot() of a test or a diffusion.
  • {goldfish} and {ergm} fit the models that a formula can move to, with specify_ergm() here and specify_dynam() in goldfish.
  • {migraph} holds the book and the teaching material that uses all of these.

infernet loads manynet and netrics, so their networks and measures are available after library(infernet).

library(infernet)

Tests

A conditional uniform graph (CUG) test compares a statistic with its values on random networks of the same size and density. A configuration test keeps the degree of each node too. A quadratic assignment procedure (QAP) test relabels the nodes of the observed network, so that the ties stay as they are and only the attributes move. Each test takes a network, a statistic from netrics, any arguments of that statistic, and a number of simulations as times:

marvel <- fict_marvel |> to_uniplex("relationship") |>
  to_unsigned() |> to_giant()
test_random(marvel, net_by_heterophily, attribute = "Gender",
            times = 200, control = list(seed = 1))
test_configuration(marvel, net_by_heterophily, attribute = "Gender",
                   times = 200, control = list(seed = 1))
test_permutation(marvel, net_by_heterophily, attribute = "Gender",
                 times = 200, control = list(seed = 1))

control takes a seed, and a number of cores to run the simulations on. The same seed gives the same result, sequentially or in parallel.

Specification

A model is written as a formula. The terms on the right-hand side construct a matrix each:

Term Constructs a matrix of
ego(attr), alter(attr) the sender’s or the receiver’s value of a nodal attribute
same(attr) 1 where sender and receiver share a value
diff(attr), sim(attr) the difference, or the similarity, of a numeric attribute
tie(layer), or the name of a layer the ties of another layer of the network
recip(layer), exchange(layer) the reverse tie, in this or another layer
indeg(layer), outdeg(layer) the degree of the sender or the receiver
tertius(attr) an aggregate of an attribute over a node’s other ties
inertia, recip, trans the outcome’s own ties, in the previous wave of a panel

The same formula can be read for an MRQAP or an ERGM, and a formula written for a goldfish DyNAM can be read for either. A specify_*() function reads a formula written for any of the three models, rewrites each term with its equivalent in its own model, and drops, with a warning, each term that its model cannot fit:

# An ergm formula, read for an MRQAP
specify_mrqap(advice ~ edges + mutual + nodematch("dept") + edgecov("friends"))
#> # An MRQAP formula read from a formula for ergm
#> 
#> advice ~ recip + same(dept) + friends
#> 
#> # adapted edges: is the intercept that the model always has
#> # adapted mutual -> recip
#> # adapted nodematch("dept") -> same(dept)
#> # adapted edgecov("friends") -> friends
# A goldfish formula, written for ergm
specify_ergm(advice ~ ego(age) + same(dept) + recip + trans)
#> # An ergm formula read from a formula for goldfish
#> 
#> advice ~ edges + nodeocov("age") + nodematch("dept") + mutual + 
#>     ttriple
#> 
#> # adapted ego(age) -> nodeocov("age")
#> # adapted same(dept) -> nodematch("dept")
#> # adapted recip -> mutual
#> # adapted trans -> ttriple

tidy() of a specification gives one row for each term, with what the model makes of it on a network:

spec <- specify_mrqap(advice ~ ego(age) + same(dept) + recip(friends) + inertia,
                      ison_hightech)
tidy(spec, ison_hightech)[, c("term", "status", "reason")]
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   term           status reason                                                  
#>   <chr>          <chr>  <chr>                                                   
#> 1 ego(age)       fits   <NA>                                                    
#> 2 same(dept)     fits   <NA>                                                    
#> 3 recip(friends) fits   <NA>                                                    
#> 4 inertia        drops  needs a longitudinal network, where it reads the outcom~

With a network as .data, specify_ergm() also gives the matrices of the terms that ergm has no name for, so that ergm::ergm() can fit the formula that it returns.

Regression

estimate_mrqap() fits a regression to a network, and permutes the nodes to find the p-value of each coefficient. By default it uses Dekker, Krackhardt, and Snijders’ (2007) double semi-partialling, which permutes the residuals of each predictor:

networkers <- ison_networkers |> to_subgraph(Discipline == "Sociology")
model <- estimate_mrqap(weight ~ ego(Citations) + alter(Citations) + sim(Citations),
                        networkers, times = 200, control = list(seed = 1))
model
#> # Linear MRQAP of weight
#> 
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   term            estimate statistic p.value signif   
#>   <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   <noquote>
#> 1 (Intercept)        2.93      0.242 <NA>             
#> 2 ego_Citations     -0.269    -1.69  0.48             
#> 3 alter_Citations   -0.158    -0.997 0.51             
#> 4 sim_Citations     39.4       3.13  0.04    *        
#> 
#> # Null: 200 permutations of each predictor, by double semi-partialling.
#> # Controls: seed = 1
#> # Signif. codes: *** 0.001, ** 0.01, * 0.05, . 0.1

control_mrqap() holds the other choices of the model: the family, what the permutations permute, robust standard errors, how to treat missing data, and the cores to run on. The family is read from the outcome when control does not give one.

control_mrqap(family = "poisson", permute = "outcome", seed = 1)
#> # Controls for an MRQAP: 3 set, 12 at their defaults
#> 
#>   permute  "outcome"
#>   family   "poisson"
#>   seed     1

A formula adds random intercepts as lme4 does, and absorbs fixed effects after a bar, as fixest does:

estimate_mrqap(weight ~ sim(Citations) + (1 | sender) + (1 | receiver),
               networkers, times = 50, control = list(seed = 1))
estimate_mrqap(weight ~ sim(Citations) | sender + receiver,
               networkers, times = 50, control = list(seed = 1))

A cognitive social structure (CSS) records each person’s report of the whole network. estimate_mrqap() reads a CSS from the network itself, and fits one observation for each sender, receiver, and reporter. The reporter terms describe the person who made the report:

css <- estimate_mrqap(advice ~ same(dept) + reports + reporter_ego,
                      ison_hightech, times = 50, control = list(seed = 1))
tidy(css)[, c("term", "estimate", "p.value")]

A longitudinal network is fitted as a panel. Each wave after the first is an outcome, and one permutation relabels the nodes in the same way in every wave. inertia, recip, and trans then read the previous wave:

panel <- estimate_mrqap(like ~ inertia + recip + same(groups),
                        ison_monks, times = 50, control = list(seed = 1))
tidy(panel)[, c("term", "estimate", "p.value")]

An unobserved tie is missing, not absent. By default, the model drops each unobserved dyad, and permutes the nodes only among nodes with the same unobserved cells, so that every permutation uses the same dyads as the observed model. control_mrqap(missing = "fail") stops instead. One student in the second wave of Knecht’s classmates did not report:

classmates <- to_wave(ison_classmates, 2)
missing <- estimate_mrqap(friends ~ ego(sex) + alter(sex) + same(sex),
                          classmates, times = 50, control = list(seed = 1))
glance(missing)[, c("nobs", "permute", "times")]

test_parameter() tests one or more coefficients together, such as the levels of a categorical attribute. test_time() tests whether coefficients are the same in each wave of a panel.

Diffusion

play_diffusions() simulates a diffusion on a network many times. test_distributions() tests whether two models of diffusion differ, and test_gof() tests whether a model fits an observed diffusion:

fast <- play_diffusions(ison_adolescents, transmissibility = 0.5,
                        times = 40, control = list(seed = 1))
slow <- play_diffusions(ison_adolescents, transmissibility = 0.2,
                        times = 40, control = list(seed = 1))
test_distributions(fast, slow, times = 200)
observed <- as_diffusion(play_diffusion(ison_adolescents, transmissibility = 0.2))
test_gof(slow, observed)

test_gof() also tests the fit of a network regression to a statistic of the observed network, from the outcomes that the model simulates.

Results

tidy() gives one row for each coefficient, and glance() one row for the model. Both work on a regression and on a test, and both give a tibble that other tools can read:

tidy(model)[, c("term", "estimate", "statistic", "p.value")]
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   term            estimate statistic p.value
#>   <chr>              <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)        2.93      0.242   NA   
#> 2 ego_Citations     -0.269    -1.69     0.48
#> 3 alter_Citations   -0.158    -0.997    0.51
#> 4 sim_Citations     39.4       3.13     0.04
glance(model)[, c("r.squared", "nobs", "permute", "times")]
#> # A tibble: 1 x 4
#>   r.squared  nobs permute   times
#>       <dbl> <int> <chr>     <dbl>
#> 1    0.0674   272 predictor   200

predict() gives the fitted value of each dyad, or of new data:

predict(model, data.frame(ego_Citations = 10, alter_Citations = 50,
                          sim_Citations = 0.5))
#> [1] 12.0213

autograph draws a test or a diffusion with plot().

Learn more

The website has a page for every function, and two tutorials:

  • “Diversity and Regression” moves from univariate tests to network regression.
  • “Diffusion and Learning” simulates diffusions and tests their fit.

To run them interactively, install migraph and run migraph::run_tute("diversity") or migraph::run_tute("diffusion").

Design principles

infernet and the other stocnet packages aim for three things:

  • Declarative simplicity: functions do one clearly named thing with few arguments. For example, test_permutation() is named for the null distribution it draws, and estimate_mrqap() follows the estimate_*() verb of goldfish.
  • Pleasant predictability: users can guess a function’s behaviour from its family. For example, the test_*() functions all take a network, a statistic, and a number of times.
  • Graceful inclusivity: functions accept whatever network users bring and return something they can use. For example, estimate_mrqap() works on any network that manynet can convert, one-mode or two-mode, and keeps missing data missing.

See the contributing guide for how these principles translate into rules for the package.

Installation

Development

infernet is not yet on CRAN. The latest binary releases for all major OSes – Windows, Mac, and Linux – can be found here. Download the appropriate binary for your operating system, and install using an adapted version of the following commands:

  • For Windows: install.packages("~/Downloads/infernet_winOS.zip", repos = NULL)
  • For Mac: install.packages("~/Downloads/infernet_macOS.tgz", repos = NULL)
  • For Unix: install.packages("~/Downloads/infernet_linuxOS.tar.gz", repos = NULL)

To install from source, please install the remotes package from CRAN and then:

  • For latest stable version: remotes::install_github("stocnet/infernet")
  • For latest development version: remotes::install_github("stocnet/infernet@develop")
